title: Ozempic Maker Novo Nordisk Taps Anthropic's AI to Speed Drug Discovery
excerpt: The Danish drugmaker will test Claude models and the new Claude Science platform in its R&D workflows, its second AI-lab alliance this year after OpenAI.
body:
• Novo Nordisk will test Anthropic's Claude models and the new Claude Science platform in its research and development workflows to accelerate discovery and development of new medicines.
  • The Ozempic and Wegovy maker will also use Anthropic's frontier models to strengthen AI-driven software development, with the collaboration designed around robust data governance and human oversight.
  • The deal follows Novo's April partnership with OpenAI and its AI co-innovation hub with Amazon Web Services in London; Goldman Sachs estimates AI could save the pharma industry up to $400 billion over the next decade.

Novo Nordisk, the Danish drugmaker behind the blockbuster diabetes and weight-loss drugs Ozempic and Wegovy, has partnered with Anthropic to use the AI lab's Claude models to speed up the discovery and development of new medicines, the companies said Wednesday.

Under the pact, Novo will initially test Anthropic's models and Claude Science, its science-focused platform, in research and development workflows, targeting scientific problems where their combined capabilities can have the greatest impact. The Wegovy maker will also deploy Anthropic's frontier models to strengthen AI-driven software development across the company.

Why Novo is betting on AI

"AI can help us increase productivity in R&D and compress the path from research to marketed product," Novo chief executive Mike Doustdar said. "But beyond this, AI tools can also offer completely new scientific opportunities and aid reasoning and understanding of human biology and drug mechanics."

Novo is already using Claude to automate clinical trial report generation and has cut the timeline for creating patient documentation from months to minutes, the companies said. The collaboration has been designed with robust data governance and human oversight, they added.

"By giving leading researchers access to safe, capable, and trusted frontier models, we can shorten research timelines, improve outcomes, and discover medicines and treatments that significantly improve human life," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said.

A crowded race across pharma

The Anthropic deal is the latest in a string of AI alliances by Novo, which partnered with OpenAI in April to apply its models to data analysis and the identification of potential drug candidates, and more recently named Amazon Web Services as its strategic partner for an AI "co-innovation hub" in London.

It is also part of a broader industry wave. Eli Lilly, Merck and Roche are all placing large bets that AI can compress drug discovery timelines and improve the odds of success for experimental drugs, while Google Cloud serves as the core AI infrastructure for Bayer and Merck. Anthropic itself has built an internal drug-discovery program focused on neglected diseases such as rare genetic disorders and tropical maladies.

AI can help us increase productivity in R&D and compress the path from research to marketed product. — Mike Doustdar, CEO, Novo Nordisk

Hope, hype and the long road to proof

The economics are compelling on paper. Goldman Sachs projects AI could save the industry up to $400 billion over the next decade by cutting costs, accelerating development and boosting success rates. But the payoff is years away: it takes eight to 10 years on average to bring a single drug from laboratory discovery through clinical trials and regulatory approval, and more than 90% of drug candidates fail during development.

For now, the industry's biggest direct gains from AI have been in automating routine work — synthesizing research, analyzing large datasets, designing human studies and identifying trial participants — rather than in discovering new medicines. Some AI-discovered candidates are being tested in humans, but no drug discovered by AI has yet won regulatory approval.

The announcement also lands amid a noisy debate over the technology's risks. Amodei has emerged as one of the industry's most vocal advocates for guardrails, warning in an essay last week that swarms of ultra-capable, autonomous AI agents "could be capable of taking over the entire internet" — a stance that has drawn sharp criticism from Microsoft's AI chief (see The Videshi's separate coverage) even as the same models are being handed to drug researchers.

What to watch next

Investors will be watching whether Novo can translate AI-assisted research into actual pipeline assets faster than rivals — and whether the Novo-Anthropic partnership produces the kind of targeted drug-discovery workflows the companies promise. With competition in the obesity-drug market intensifying and Novo's patent cliffs approaching, the R&D engine the company builds now will determine what it sells a decade from now.
